tip: For transport Dutch uses 'met': 'met de trein' = by train, also 'met de bus', 'met de auto'.
Boats 'varen', not 'rijden': 'de veerboot vaart' = the ferry sails.
'Net' means just now, a very recent event: 'zijn net getrouwd' = just got married.
'Begon' is the past of 'beginnen', a verb that changes its vowel in the past.
'Smaken' pairs with 'naar' for flavours: 'smaakt naar vanille' = tastes of vanilla.
'Last hebben van' = to be bothered by or suffer from: 'last van hooikoorts'.
'Het zat zijn' = to be fed up: 'ik ben het zat' – informal but common.
'Zich bezighouden met' = to be busy with something: 'bezighouden ons met het schilderen'.
'Zijn' means both 'to be' and 'his' – context distinguishes them.
'Elkaar' is one fixed word for each other: 'we elkaar hebben gezien'.
'Ons' is the possessive for het-words: 'ons huis', while de-words take 'onze'.
'Zullen' builds the future and sends the infinitive to the end: 'zullen ... bekijken'.
In the present perfect the participle lands at the very end, so 'gehoord' follows both 'hebben' and 'niets'.
For the future, 'zullen' takes a plain infinitive and pushes it to the end: 'zullen ... schoonmaken'.
'Zal' is the singular of 'zullen'; use 'zal' with 'hij', 'zij' (she) or 'ik', and 'zullen' with 'wij' or a plural subject.
How-are-you is fixed as 'hoe gaat het met je', literally how goes it with you; 'je' is the casual you.
When an adverb like 'helaas' opens the sentence, the verb comes before the subject: 'helaas kan ik', not 'helaas ik kan'.
With a helper verb like 'kan', 'niet' sits just before the final infinitive: 'kan ... niet vinden'.
'Niet' sits just before the closing infinitive, so it lands right ahead of 'oplossen' at the end.
After 'een' with a de-word the adjective takes -e, and 'tuin' is a de-word, so you get 'een mooie tuin'.
'Meisje' is a het-word, so it is 'het meisje', not 'de', even though it means girl.
'Half negen' means 8:30, not 9:30; Dutch 'half X' counts half an hour before X, not after.
Chasing wraps around the noun: 'achter' goes before 'de kat' and 'aan' after it, giving 'achter de kat aan'.
With 'een' plus a het-word the adjective stays bare, so it is 'een mooi boek', not 'mooie', since 'boek' is a het-word.
Open with an adverb and Dutch puts the verb before the subject: 'gelukkig kwam de bus' (fortunately came the bus), unlike English.
Use 'geen', not 'niet', to say no before a noun: 'geen tijd' means no time or not any time.
Regular verbs form the past with -de or -te, and the plural adds -n: 'verhuisden' = moved.
'Last hebben van' means to be bothered by, and 'nergens' replaces the object: 'nergens last van' = bothered by nothing.
Dutch marks an upright position with 'staan', so a bike 'staat in de schuur' where English just says is.
Comparatives add -er and pair with 'dan' for than: 'moeilijker dan verwacht' means harder than expected.
